analysis.one_liner: Requires pharmacy benefit managers to disclose drug pricing, rebates, and fees to employers and patients.
analysis.headline: Introduced in March 2025 with support from both parties, the bill has received no hearing, markup, or vote in any of its three assigned committees.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would force pharmacy benefit managers — the middlemen that negotiate drug prices for employers and insurers — to report every six months what they charge plans, what they pay pharmacies, and how much they keep in rebates, fees, and discounts. It would also expose when plans steer patients to pharmacies owned by the same company managing the benefit, and requirePBMs to disclose fees paid to brokers who refer them business. Plans would have to share summary information with patients on request.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers and workers with job-based health plans, who currently cannot see the difference between what their plan pays a pharmacy benefit manager and what that manager pays the pharmacy — a gap known as 'spread pricing.' Large employers (100 or more employees) would get claims-level detail every six months, including the median and lowest prices for drugs when the same prescription is filled by an affiliated versus independent pharmacy. Patients could request a summary document and their own claims-level spread information.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Employers, workers, and patients with job-based coverage

how_it_helps.text: Pharmacy benefit managers must report at least twice a year, for each drug, the difference between what the plan pays them and what they pay the pharmacy, plus all rebates, fees, and discounts they receive from manufacturers and group purchasing organizations.

Plans must explain any benefit design that steers patients to mail-order, specialty, or retail pharmacies owned by or affiliated with the pharmacy benefit manager, and report the percentage of prescriptions those affiliates dispense and how their prices compare with independent pharmacies in the network.
Patients may request an aggregate summary document and the claims-level price spread for their own prescriptions, and plans must notify participants yearly that these reports exist.

The bill requires disclosure of payments to brokers, consultants, and advisers for referring or retaining pharmacy benefit management business, and sets civil penalties of $10,000 per day for failure to report and up to $100,000 per item of knowingly false information.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmacy benefit managers and the mail-order and specialty pharmacies they own, which bear compliance costs and see their current pricing practices — spread pricing, rebate retention, and affiliate pharmacy markups — opened up to the employers and regulators who pay for them. Some compliance cost could be passed back to plans as higher fees.
analysis.who_pays_short: Pharmacy benefit managers and their affiliated pharmacies

drawbacks.text: Transparency alone does not cap prices. Employers and patients would see the spreads and markups, but nothing in the bill limits them, so savings depend on plans and employers using the disclosed information to renegotiate.
The requirements do not take effect until 30 months after enactment, and the Department of Health and Human Services must first write rules setting the report format, delaying any benefit further.

The most detailed, claims-level reporting applies only to plans offered by large employers or large plans of 100 or more participants; smaller employers get only summary documents, so most small businesses would not see the full picture.

Pharmacy benefit managers and some health economists argue that publishing rebate and discount data could weaken negotiations or push manufacturers to raise list prices, and compliance costs could be passed through to plans as higher fees — costs that employers would have to weigh against the value of the information.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For employers and patients, the benefit is real but indirect: this bill shines a light on opaque pricing rather than lowering it directly. Its main power is arming large employers to renegotiate. The strongest objections — a 30-month delay, rules-writing lag, limited reach to small employers, and the risk that disclosure raises list prices or compliance fees — are honest limits on how much it would accomplish, not reasons the bill serves anyone but the pharmacy benefit managers it regulates.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to three House committees on the day it was introduced and has sat there with no hearing, markup, or floor vote since.

narrative.text: Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet introduced the bill on March 27, 2025, joined in the original sponsorship by Rep. Buddy Carter of Georgia and Rep. John James (Republicans) and Rep. Rob Menendez (Democrat).
The bill was referred the same day to the House Energy and Commerce, Education and Workforce, and Ways and Means Committees, and no further action has been recorded since.
It has three cosponsors: two Republicans and one Democrat.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmacy benefit managers and the affiliated pharmacies they own, whose pricing and rebate arrangements remain out of employers' and patients' sight for now. Three companies — CVS Caremark, Express Scripts, and Optum Rx — process the large majority of American prescriptions, so inaction leaves a concentrated industry's current economics in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pharmacy benefit managers and their affiliated pharmacies

against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and has taken no recorded action on the bill since.

against.name: Pharmacy benefit manager industry (CVS Caremark, Express Scripts, Optum Rx)
against.what_they_did: The major pharmacy benefit managers have consistently opposed mandates to disclose their rebate and pricing arrangements to plan sponsors.

sides.party_line_note: The original sponsorship was split between one Democrat and two Republicans, and its three cosponsors include two Republicans and one Democrat; no recorded votes have occurred.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers (CVS Caremark, Express Scripts, Optum Rx)
industries.note: The bill would expose the spread between what plans pay PBMs and what PBMs pay pharmacies, plus the rebates and fees PBMs keep — the core of their current business economics. PBMs' interest in keeping those arrangements confidential runs against employers' and patients' interest in seeing them.

The bill would require disclosure of how plans steer patients to pharmacies owned by the PBM and how affiliate prices compare with independent pharmacies in the same network, undercutting a key profit channel.

Community pharmacists have long argued that PBMs underpay them while steering patients to affiliated pharmacies; the disclosure of affiliate dispensing shares and price comparisons gives them evidence to press for fairer reimbursement.
The bill would require disclosure of referral and retention fees paid to brokers and advisers, a compensation stream that currently shapes which PBM an employer hires without the employer seeing it.

industries.industry: Health insurers (many of which own PBMs)
industries.note: Insurers would receive more detailed reports from PBMs, but the largest insurers own the biggest PBMs, so disclosure aimed at the PBM also reaches their own vertically integrated operations.

analysis.trajectory: With only three cosponsors and no committee action since March 2025, this bill is unlikely to advance on its own this Congress. PBM transparency provisions are more likely to become law if attached to a larger health or spending package — a common path for measures sitting in multiple committees.
